//: A Gatehouse configuration covering every provider kind this build supports.
Pass it with:  gatehouse --config ./samples/gatehouse.json
Every setting can also come from an environment variable using the
Gatehouse__Section__Key form, for example:
Gatehouse__Store__ConnectionString='Data Source=/var/lib/gatehouse/gatehouse.db'
Keys beginning with // are comments. JSON has none, and .NET configuration ignores
unrecognised properties, so this is the least surprising convention available.
One catch, and it bites: Providers and Models are DICTIONARIES, not objects. Every
key inside them is data, so a '//' there binds as a provider or a model literally
named '//' and startup validation rejects it. Comment individual entries from
inside, as below - never the Providers or Models block itself.
About Models: the key is what callers put in the 'model' field. Keeping it separate
from the upstream name is what lets you move traffic between providers - even
between vendors - without any application redeploying.
Exact-match response caching. OFF by default and left off here, deliberately:
caching changes observable behaviour. Repeated identical requests stop reaching the
provider, so they stop being sampled and start returning a fixed answer. That is
usually wanted - but not as a surprise after an upgrade.
Exact match ONLY. Gatehouse never serves an answer to a question that merely
resembles a stored one; see docs/caching.md for why semantic caching is a Phase 4
question rather than a quick win.
A cache hit is never counted as provider usage. The tokens are real but nobody was
billed, so 'gatehouse usage' reports them as avoided rather than as spend.
Cache.//MaxEntries: With MaxResponseBytes this is the memory bound: worst case is roughly the product of the two.
Cache.//ScopeToOrganisation: On by default. Costs hit rate, and stops one tenant's spend subsidising another's. Turn it off for a single-tenant deployment.

//: Fallback chains and circuit breakers. The defaults are chosen so that turning
this on changes nothing for a healthy deployment - a breaker that opens under
normal operation is worse than no breaker, because it turns provider latency
into gateway outages and teaches operators to switch the feature off.
Fallbacks are inert unless a route declares them; see 'fast' below.
The breaker is keyed per provider AND upstream model, not per provider. On Azure
quota is per deployment, so a saturated gpt-4o deployment must not take out the
gpt-4o-mini deployment beside it.
Resilience.//FailureRatio: Open when this fraction of the window failed. Half means 'down', not 'degraded'.
Resilience.//MinimumThroughput: Ignore the ratio until the window holds this many calls, so one failure on a quiet gateway is not a 100% failure rate.
Resilience.//BreakDurationSeconds: How long an open circuit refuses traffic before admitting one probe.
Resilience.//MaxAttempts: The most upstream calls one client request may cause, including the first. A safety rail: without it a long chain against an outage multiplies one request into that many billed calls.

Store.//: SQLite is the default and needs no external database. WAL is enabled automatically.

//: Required is the default. A gateway with no keys refuses to start rather than
starting and rejecting every request - the failure mode that looks healthy to an
orchestrator. Issue one with:  gatehouse keys create --name my-app
Set to Disabled for local development, or where something in front of the gateway
authenticates callers. Gatehouse warns on every startup in that mode, because it
holds your provider credentials.
Kind 'openai-compatible' serves OpenAI itself and anything that speaks its API:
Ollama, vLLM and Foundry Local included.
Prefer ApiKeyEnvironmentVariable over a literal ApiKey. A key written into a config
file ends up in git history, in container images, and in every backup of both.
Gatehouse logs a warning at startup if it finds the literal form.
Azure OpenAI. The REST API is OpenAI-compatible, so the same provider serves it;
only addressing and authentication differ. UpstreamModel on a route is the
DEPLOYMENT name, which is often not the model family name.
UseManagedIdentity is the recommended setting and stores no credential at all -
nothing to rotate, nothing to leak. Set ManagedIdentityClientId as well if the host
has more than one user-assigned identity.

anthropic.//: Authenticates with x-api-key rather than a bearer token; Gatehouse handles that.

google.//: The key travels in the x-goog-api-key header, never in a query string.

ollama.//: Local models need no credential at all.

gpt-4o-mini.//: Alias and upstream model match, so UpstreamModel can be omitted.

//: A capability name. Repoint it at another model or vendor at will.
Fallbacks are tried in order when the primary fails in a way the upstream is
responsible for - a timeout, a 429, a 5xx. A malformed request is NOT retried
elsewhere: it would be malformed at the next provider too, and trying it there
bills a second account to produce the same rejection.
The list is the whole chain and is not followed transitively. If 'claude-sonnet'
declares its own fallbacks they are not reached from here, so what you read on
this entry is every route a request for 'fast' can touch.
Cross-vendor fallback changes which model answers. Configure it where the caller
wants an answer more than a specific model, and not where output must be
reproducible.

gpt-4o-azure.//: For Azure, UpstreamModel is the deployment name.
